A second bridge to avoid depending on one

A bridge joins two segments, but it runs on electricity: if it is turned off, the segments are left disconnected. It is a point of failure.

The natural idea is to add a second bridge in parallel. Let's see what happens when X (bottom) sends a frame to Y (top):

  • The frame reaches both bridges.
  • Both do forwarding, because the destination is on the other segment.
  • Since the upper segment is shared, A and B compete for access to the medium.
Bridges are transparent: neither knows the other exists.
Two paths between the same segments: there is redundancy… and two copies of the same frame waiting to go up.
The copy comes in the wrong side

One of the bridges wins the medium. Say it is A: it transmits the frame on the upper segment and Y receives it.

But bridge B also receives it, from the other side. It sees a frame from X arriving from above and draws false conclusions:

  • It thinks X is on the upper segment.
  • It will look for Y on the lower segment.

Its table is left with information that isn't real.
With two paths, the same source address shows up on both sides of the bridge.
Both entries are backwards: X is below and Y above.

B still had its copy ready to transmit, and now it has also received the same frame from above. It transmits it downward, and the same thing happens to bridge A: it receives it from the opposite side and gets confused the same way.

This repeats: one wins and transmits, the other passes the same message again… an infinite loop at the data link layer.

The network is completely knocked out: the bridges block it by sending the same frame back and forth.
At the data link layer nothing stops a frame that goes around: the loop doesn't break on its own.
The same frame goes from one segment to the other endlessly. The other stations can no longer use the network.
Spanning Tree: get to know each other and close a port

The underlying problem is that bridges don't know about each other. For that the Spanning Tree protocol (STP) was created: it detects loops and breaks them.

The bridges discover each other and agree on who operates and who closes an interface, so as not to receive the same message from both sides.

Redundancy isn't lost: if the operating bridge goes down, the other detects it and takes over its role.
STP doesn't eliminate the redundant path: it keeps it in reserve, blocked.
Only one path remains active between the segments. The frame arrives once and the loop disappears.
Switches have the same problem: BPDUs

In a star topology there are also loops: it is enough for three switches to be connected in a triangle.

To detect it, each switch continuously sends, out all its ports, a BPDU (Bridge PDU): a message that says which switch it is. It is sent every 2 seconds.

With the BPDUs each switch knows it has other switches connected. Once they know each other, they run the Spanning Tree algorithm to decide how to break the loop.
Loops come from ignorance; BPDUs are the way to introduce yourself.
Every 2 seconds, each switch sends a BPDU out each port with its Bridge ID.
Electing the root: the lowest Bridge ID

The idea is to turn the loop into a tree: one switch is chosen as the root (ROOT) and the rest are branches that don't close the cycle.

Every switch has a Bridge ID, made up of a priority and its MAC address. The one with the lowest priority is the ROOT; if all have the same priority, the MAC breaks the tie.

The BPDU carries its own Bridge ID and also the Root ID, so everyone agrees on who the ROOT is. Everyone takes part in the election.
The ROOT doesn't block any of its ports.
Switch 3 has the lowest priority (10): it is the ROOT even though its MAC is the highest.

Each switch that is not the ROOT identifies the port that leads to the root by the shortest path (direct or through other switches): that is its ROOT PORT.

Switches 1 and 2 are also connected to each other. They must break the tie: one keeps the port active and the other blocks it. Here switch 1 loses, the one with the higher Bridge ID.

No messages are sent or received through the closed port: the link is left for BPDUs only. To go from 1 to 2 you have to pass through the ROOT.
Tree = a single path between any two switches, always going through the root.
The frame from A to B goes down to the ROOT and back up. The 1–2 link exists, but carries no data.
A link goes down: STP recalculates

Spanning Tree discovers loops and disables redundant links, but doesn't forget about them.

If a link is disconnected, the algorithm recalculates to see what happened and reactivates the link it had blocked.

In the example, the link between switch 2 and the ROOT goes down. Switch 1 unblocks its port, and switch 2 reaches the root through 1: the shortest path it has left.
The blocked link is the spare: it goes into service when the primary one fails.
With no loop there is nothing to block: the two remaining links form the tree.
Plugging in something new: a port's states

All switches run STP on all their ports. When a new device is connected, the switch has to see what got connected before activating the port, so as not to create another loop. The port goes through a series of states:

  • BLOCKING: doesn't let traffic through.
  • LISTENING: listens to what is on the other side.
  • LEARNING: learns the device's MAC.
  • FORWARDING: passes traffic, or blocks if a loop would occur.
Listen first, forward later: a new port never starts out passing traffic.
Listens to see whether a switch, a workstation, etc. was connected.
Learns the MAC address of the connected device.
Passes traffic, or blocks the port if a loop occurs.
If while listening it finds a BPDU, there is a new switch on the network. If its priority is lower, it becomes the ROOT, the previous one stops being it and the topology changes.

• Two paths between the same segments = corrupt tables and an infinite loop at the data link layer.
  • Switches introduce themselves with BPDUs every 2 seconds.
  • Bridge ID = priority + MAC. The lowest is the ROOT.
  • Each switch picks its root port; the leftover links are blocked (only BPDUs pass).
  • If a link goes down, it recalculates and the blocked one is reactivated.
  • New port: blocking → listening → learning → forwarding.

So far all the stations on a switch share the same broadcast domain. In the next lesson we split it into several with VLANs.

The first one that was powered on
The one with the most stations connected

What can pass through a port that Spanning Tree left blocked?
All traffic, but with lower priority
The link is disabled for sending and receiving messages, but BPDUs keep passing: that's how it detects whether it must be reactivated.
Why doesn't a newly connected port go straight to FORWARDING?
Because it must first listen to what got connected, so as not to create a loop
Because the cable needs to charge
Because it waits for the ROOT to assign it a MAC
Because it must negotiate the speed at 10 Mbps
The port starts in BLOCKING, listens (LISTENING) in case a BPDU from another switch shows up, learns the MAC (LEARNING) and only then forwards.
Two paths between the same segments: the frame is forwarded endlessly and the MAC tables end up wrong. It knocks out the network.
Discovers loops and disables redundant links, forming a tree rooted at the ROOT. If a link fails, it recalculates.
